# CS6750 Individual Project

## Chase Hasbrouck chasbrouck3@gatech.edu

***Abstract—***This project focuses on the intersection of human-computer interaction and cybersecurity, focusing on enhancing the user experience of the open source network security tool Wireshark. Through comprehensive needfinding activities, this project identified areas for enhancement, leading to the development and iterative refinement of design prototypes. Ultimately, the final prototype was found to be a statistically significant improvement over the original interface. 

# **1 INTRODUCTION**

Computer security, or cybersecurity as it is now more commonly known, is a core domain that is vital to any major enterprise. Unfortunately, many cybersecurity tools have had little attention paid to their interface, as they are largely used by experts, not beginners. This contributes to the shortage of trained cybersecurity professionals, as the learning curve for beginners is very high.

For this project, I would like to focus on a common task for  network security: analyzing a packet capture. A packet capture, or PCAP, typically contains information about every single network packet that has traveled over a given network link where a capture device has been applied. There are many tools for this, but the most commonly used tool is the open-source tool [Wireshark](https://www.wireshark.org/).  

A key task when working with PCAPs is filtering them to the packets of interest, as they can number in the millions of packets. Depicted below in Figure 1 is an example of a Wireshark display filter in action. The packet capture in question has been filtered by typing the text “tcp” into the filter box, which causes Wireshark to filter out all traffic from the capture that isn’t part of the TCP protocol. 

I believe there is significant room for improvement on this task from an HCI perspective. I periodically teach a class on network security, and I find myself commonly having to explain how to perform this task in Wireshark repeatedly, as new users frequently make errors when performing it. To address these challenges, this project employs a design lifecycle approach to enhance this task, aiming to simplify display filter application for novices, while preserving functionality for expert users.

***Figure 1—***An example of a Wireshark display filter in action. Source: [Wireshark manual](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/wsug_html_chunked/ChWorkDisplayFilterSection.html).

# **2 NEEDFINDING PLAN**

I have three separate needfinding activities planned for this project.

## **2.1 Needfinding Activity 1: Interviews with co-workers**

My current job is in cybersecurity for one of the branches of the U.S. military. As such, I have close links to 10-20 people who use Wireshark on a regular basis, as well as 100-200 who perform similar cybersecurity activities but do not actively use Wireshark. I plan to recruit 5-10 of these individuals for interviews, using a combination of email invitations, posts on internal discussion groups, and personal interaction.  During the interview, I will ask them several questions about their use of Wireshark and their opinions on the existing filtering mechanism. 

There is risk of voluntary response bias by only selecting individuals who are willing to participate; observer bias given that I have a previous relationship with the individuals in question; and recall bias given that not all participants may have used Wireshark recently. I am unable to mitigate the voluntary response bias, but I will mitigate the observer bias by using a pre-written script and attempting to minimize my direct involvement with the interviewees, and I will mitigate the recall bias by providing screenshots of the Wireshark interface. Despite the biases, the detailed feedback available from users who are proficient in this tool is worth collecting.

## **2.2 Needfinding Activity 2: Surveys of classmates** 

To supplement Needfinding Activity 1, I will survey classmates to gather their opinions on Wireshark’s filtering capabilities. I will recruit this cohort using the built-in tools within the class (PeerSurvey and the course forum), as well as a post on the unofficial course Slack channel. 

There is a risk of voluntary response bias and recall bias. The class incentives for students to participate will mitigate voluntary response bias. I will add screenshots of Wireshark directly to the survey to reduce recall bias.

## **2.3 Needfinding Activity 3: Heuristic evaluation** 

Separate from the user-involved needfinding activities, I will conduct a heuristic evaluation. I will focus on the following three heuristics, derived from [Nielsen’s ten heuristics](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/) (Nielsen, 2014):

1. **Visibility of system status:** Does the design keep users informed about what is going on through appropriate feedback?  
2. **Error prevention:** Does the design prevent problems from occurring, or check for them and offer assistance?  
3. **Recognition rather than recall:** Does the design minimize the user’s memory load by making elements, actions, and options visible?

# **3 NEEDFINDING RESULTS**

## **3.1 Needfinding Results 1: Interview with co-workers**

After soliciting a large pool of co-workers, I was only able to find 3 people who were willing to answer my questions. Below is a summary of the findings from each interview. The list of questions asked is provided in Appendix 1\.

### ***3.1.1 Interview with Person \#1***

Person \#1 described themselves as a “beginner” with Wireshark. They said that using the basic filters was pretty easy, but they frequently misremembered the specific spelling of certain filters or syntax, such as needing two equals characters for comparisons instead of one. They would ask Google for a “Wireshark cheatsheet” when needed to help remind them of the syntax. They did not use any of the other filter features. They were unaware that Wireshark displays context-sensitive error messages at the bottom of the screen or filtered packet counts, and was surprised that nobody had pointed this out to them before.

### ***3.1.2 Interview with Person \#2***

Person \#2 described themselves as “reasonably proficient” with Wireshark, though they “don’t use it much anymore.” They stated that they felt the filters worked well, and wouldn’t change much. When asked to be specific, they mentioned that they liked how the input box turns red for an invalid filter, and green for a valid filter. They did not use any of the other filter features. They were aware of the context-sensitive error messages, but preferred copying filters from an authoritative source to avoid syntax errors. They were not aware of the filtered packet count, but did not think it was particularly useful. 

### ***3.1.3 Interview with Person \#3***

Person \#3 described themselves as a “frequent user” of Wireshark. They stated the filter syntax was logical and powerful. They mentioned that they used to have a separate text file of filter strings, but had recently realized that clicking the bookmark icon next to the filter box popped up a menu that allowed you to save filters for re-use. They were aware of the contextual error messages, and referenced them frequently. They were aware of the filtered packet count and used it frequently to help determine if they had filtered correctly.

## **3.3 Needfinding Results 3: Heuristic Evaluation Results**

I chose three of Nielsen’s ten heuristics to evaluate the Wireshark display filter. 

### ***3.3.1 Visibility of System Status***

The display filter does a poor job of communicating system status. It is not very clear when a filter has been successfully applied. For example, when a user types in a filter and applies it, the only indication that a change has occurred is the change in text at the bottom right indicating the number of packets filtered, and missing entries in the list of packets. A more egregious example is a filter that is applied successfully but filters no packets (e.g. all packets pass); in that case, there is **no** visual confirmation that the filter was applied successfully. See Figure 2 and Figure 3..  

![][image2]

***Figure 2—***A typed-in display filter, before applying.

 ![][image3]

***Figure 3—***A typed-in display filter, after applying.

### ***3.3.2 Error Prevention***

The display does a good job of error prevention. The most notable design element here is the coloration of the design filter box. When a filter is being typed, the filter box turns red to indicate that the filter has an error, and a helpful error message is displayed (See Figure 4). When the error is corrected, the filter box turns green to indicate the problem has cleared. However, this design could still be improved; the color filter only protects against syntax errors and the informational message is displayed far away from the filter box, making it tough for new users to understand that the informational message is connected to the filters.

![][image4]

***Figure 4—***An incorrectly typed-in display filter.

### ***3.3.3 Recognition Rather than Recall***

The display does a mixed job of fostering recognition rather than recall. When typing in a filter, the display pops up a context-aware list of possible completions, which definitely aids recognition. However, that is the limit of the aid provided in this area; there is no help provided with syntax correction, and the context-awareness is strict, which can be confusing. For example, the correct syntax for referencing destination IP addresses is “ip.dst”; typing “ip.d” will bring up the text completion, but “ip.destination” will bring up no suggestions. 

# **4 INITIAL BRAINSTORMING PLAN**

The initial brainstorming phase will begin with a review of the needfinding outcomes. The goal is to identify clear challenges experienced by users in order to set an agenda for the brainstorming session.

Following this preparatory phase, I will brainstorm by attempting to generate as many ideas as possible in a 15 minute span. This time constraint is specifically chosen to encourage rapid idea generation. To broaden the scope of the ideas and counteract my personal bias, I will also use AI assistance (ChatGPT), using its capability to suggest ideas as well. 

# **5 BRAINSTORMING RESULTS**

The brainstorming process began with a review of needfinding efforts. I then proceeded to a rapid idea session, where I developed 16 possible ideas, combined with an AI-generated (ChatGPT) list of 25 ideas. In general, the majority of the ideas focused around making the filter easier to use and to learn, based on results from needfinding that indicated that this was  more important than introducing new features. After evaluating the results of my brainstorming, I did an initial filter for feasibility, reducing the number of possible ideas to five. 

1. **Natural Language Interface:** Allow the user to type in English what they’re looking for, and have the system automatically translate it to the correct syntax.  
2. **Filter Box Expansion**: Dynamically expand the filter input box when clicked on, to make longer expressions either to review, and allow for more contextual help to be displayed.  
3. **Move Informational Messages:** Currently, the display filter window is at the top of the window, with info messages displayed at the bottom; bringing them closer together could improve contextual understanding.  
4. **Pop-Out Pane for Help:** Add a pop-out pane for when users are typing in the filter box to bring up contextual suggestions and tips.  
5. **Tutorial:** Create an interactive tutorial on first run, featuring a seris of pop-ups that demonstrate how to create a filter and highlight where the informational messages appear.

From these ideas, I’ve narrowed the list down to three ideas that I think are the best fit to move on to prototyping, based on their feasibility, their alignment with the primary needs identified by the needfinding process, and the ability to implement with limited resources. (See Appendix 3 and 4 for the full list of brainstormed ideas, both by myself and with AI assistance.)

## **5.1 Design Alternative 1: UI Re-Arrangement**

This design alternative rearranges the current Wireshark layout to add a message display area in closer proximity to the filter input box. This will make messages more visible to users, facilitating quicker adjustments. The design alternative focuses around the idea of spatial organization, reducing the gulf of evaluation by making it more apparently clear when their filter has an error. I will have to balance this idea against the cognitive load generated by rearranging an interface that has been functionally very similar for years. 

## **5.2 Design Alternative 2: Filter Box Expansion**

This design alternative features the Wireshark layout with an expandable filter input area. When the filter box is clicked, it dynamically enlarges to accommodate longer filter expressions and provide room for the display of help or examples. This design alternative focuses around the idea of reducing cognitive load by allowing the user to better concentrate on the entry area they are working on. However, I will have to be careful to not obscure relevant data from the window that users reference to help build their display filter. 

## **5.3 Design Alternative 3: Pop-Out Pane**

This design alternative features a side panel that emerges adjacent to the filter input box, with the rest of the window dynamically resizing to compensate. This pane could offer the current contextual help in a clearer way, or offer other examples that are not able to fit within the current UI. While this provides good assistance to beginners, I will need to keep in mind that this may not be helpful to experts, and may in fact make them less efficient. To this end, this feature should be able to be disabled via Wireshark’s preferences. 

# **6 INITIAL PROTOTYPING**

![][image5]

***Figure 5—***Wireframe of Wireshark application, no changes

I elected to create low-fidelity wireframe prototypes of all three design alternatives to move on to evaluation, as well as a wireframe of the design as it currently exists to better highlight the differences. (All wireframes were  generated via [Balsamiq Wireframes](https://balsamiq.com/wireframes/).)

These prototypes are all designed around variations on a single idea; moving the contextual info/error display box, which is currently at the bottom of the display, to an area where it is more visible to a user who is currently typing into the display filter. This reduces the gulf of evaluation for a user, as it makes it more obvious for novice users that the contextual info/error display is providing relevant feedback, and increases the speed of feedback response. The existing info field will be kept as-is for non-display filter messages.  

![][image6]

***Figure 6—***Prototype 1

## **6.1 Prototype 1: Info Box Below Filter Box**

This prototype slightly shrinks the packet table downwards, adding an additional info box below the filter input box to display contextual info/errors. This is the most minimal change to the existing UI, but it also does not allow much room for more detailed info messages to be displayed.

![][image7]

***Figure 7—***Prototype 2

## **6.2 Prototype 2: Enlarged Filter Box with Accompanying Info Box**

This prototype shrinks the packet table more than in Prototype 1\. With the extra space provided, a two-pane box display is created. The filter input area is now narrowed from a long “bar” stretching the length of the window to a mid-length but taller “box.” To the right of the filter input area is a new message display “box,” which is the new location for error messages. This adds a moderate amount of room for more detailed info messages. 

![][image8]

***Figure 8—***Prototype 3

## **6.3 Prototype 3: Vertical Info Box on Left**

This prototype features a horizontal shrink instead of a vertical shrink, with all panes shrinking to the right and a new vertical info box on the left. This adds the most space for information, but offers the most dramatic change to the UI.

# **8 EVALUATION RESULTS**

## **8.1 Evaluation Results 1: Interviews with co-workers** 

Below is a summary of my findings from the prototype evaluation interviews. All interviewees were provided Figures 5-8 (above), and asked for their impressions of each prototype, in a free-response fashion. (See Appendix 5 for specific interview questions.)  

### ***8.1.1 Interview with Person \#1***

Person \#1 felt positive about Prototype \#1 and \#2, and had mixed feelings about Prototype \#3. They praised both Prototype \#1 and \#2 as being much more intuitive, but said they would have to actually “see them in action” to know which they preferred. They liked how Prototype \#3 made the errors more visible, but felt it should be on the right side of the display, not the left. I have quantified this feedback as a “4” for Prototype \#1 and \#2, and a “3” for Prototype \#3.

### ***8.1.2 Interview with Person \#2***

Person \#2 disliked all of the prototypes. They felt that all prototypes shrunk the window displaying the list of packets too much. They stated that the error info was less important once you became proficient in Wireshark, as you could see from the list of packets whether your filter was applying correctly or not and didn’t need an info message to tell you. I have quantified this feedback as a “2” for all three prototypes.

### ***8.1.3 Interview with Person \#3***

Person \#3 felt that only Prototype \#1 had merit. They criticized Prototype \#2 for narrowing the filter window, stating that complicated filters often can stretch the length of the window, and wrapping the filter onto a second line would be more confusing than the default. They strongly criticized Prototype \#3; they felt a tall, narrow window for displaying text would be unhelpful due to how much the text would have to wrap. I have quantified this feedback as a “4” for Prototype 1, a “2” for Prototype \#2, and a “1” for Prototype \#3.

### ***8.1.4 Interview Results***

Overall, Prototype \#1 was perceived as slightly better than Prototype \#2, but both prototypes were close to neutral. Prototype \#3 was slightly disliked.

# **9 SECOND ITERATION**

For the second iteration of the design lifecycle, I will refine my approach based on the lessons learned from the first iteration. This stage will focus on addressing the identified user needs and refining our three design prototypes into one final prototype. 

The evaluations revealed a clear separation in user preferences. The three individual interviews showed a slight preference for Prototype \#1, with both Prototype \#2 and \#3 being favored less than the original interface. The survey showed a moderate preference for Prototype \#2, a slight preference for Prototype \#1, and a neutral result for Prototype \#3. 

As such, the next iteration will focus on combining the feedback from both evaluation methods, and attempt to combine Prototypes \#1 and \#2 into a final prototype. Prototype \#3 will be eliminated from further consideration. 

# **10 FINAL PROTOTYPE**

Combining Prototype \#1 and \#2, the final prototype keeps the split-box from Prototype \#2, but reduces the vertical size while adding drag handles to adjust the size to the user’s preference. Additionally, a button is added to expand the filter box temporarily for long filters, while the display filter menu is reworked to enhance discoverability.

The final prototype incorporates several of the design principles espoused by Norman, Nielsen, Constantine, and Lockwood discussed in class. 

1. **Discoverability:** By adding toggleable options to the filter menu, it makes it easier for a new user to discover options without having to deep-dive into menus.  
2. **Simplicity:** Adding a “clear filter” link both makes it very apparent that a filter is applied and offers a one-click way to remove the filter.   
3. **Consistency:** Retaining the existing color-coding of the filter box input, as well as the existing menu button, reduces re-learning for existing users.  
4. **Flexibility:** The added keyboard shortcuts enable expert users to quickly switch through filters, while new users can access the same options via the filter menu.   
5. **Feedback:** By displaying information about the error directly to the right of the filter input box, the prototype makes it more intuitive that the error message is connected to the input they have just entered.  
6. **Affordances:** By adding drag arrows to the divider between the filter input box and the error display box, it is clear that the control affords adjustment as needed.

## **13.3 Comparative Evaluation of Prototypes Against Baseline** 

In assessing the perceived effectiveness of the prototypes compared to the original interface, one-sample t-tests were conducted. The overall score for each prototype was compared against a baseline value of 3.00, representing the neutral assessment of the original interface. The Final Prototype (mean=4.17, SD (pooled) \= 0.53) was rated significantly higher than the baseline with t(8) \= 6.62 and a p-value of \<0.001. Prototype \#2 (mean=3.94, SD (pooled)=0.78) is rated significantly higher than the baseline with t(7) \= 3.41 and a p-value of 0.011 at the 95% confidence level, but not at the 99% confidence level. Prototype \#1 and \#3 did not show statistically significant differences at the 95% confidence level. 

***Table 9—***Prototype Performance Analysis Against Baseline

| \# | Version | SD (pooled) | Overall (95% CI) | t-statistic | p-value |

## **Appendix 3: Personal Brainstorming**

The below is a list of ideas I came up with when allowing 15 minutes for free expression: 

1. A tutorial for new users  
2. Clippy for Wireshark  
3. Better use of color   
4. FilterChat \- a chatbot that helps with filters  
5. A natural language interface \- type what you want, the system creates the filter  
6. Aliases \- let “ip destination” work like “ip.dst”  
7. Use the mouse scroll wheel to scroll through completions  
8. Expand the box when clicked on  
9. Move the “informational messages” to a more prominent location in the UI (or at least more contextual)  
10. A pop-out pane for contextual suggestions  
11. “Other users tried…”  
12. Graphical modeling \- represent the packet capture visually, and use highlights to illuminate what is kept/not kept  
13. Draw-a-filter \- like before, but actually support drawing lines for in/out  
14. Support other common programming language syntaxes  
15. Behavior/heuristic filtering based on the user \- what type of filters does this user frequently use?  
16. Heuristic filtering based on the loaded packet capture \- suggest HTTP filters if HTTP traffic detected

## **Appendix 4: ChatGPT Brainstorming Prompt**

*User*

Act as a design consultant. You are brainstorming ideas on how to improve the Wireshark display filter. Please generate 25 ideas, without consideration for their practicality or feasibility. 

*ChatGPT*

1. Dynamic Filter Suggestions: Implement a dynamic suggestion system that offers filter options based on the user's typing and past filtering behaviors, adapting to the most commonly used protocols and fields.  
2. Natural Language Processing (NLP): Incorporate NLP to allow users to create complex filters using natural language, making the tool more accessible to beginners and non-technical users.  
3. Color-Coded Syntax: Utilize color coding for different parts of the filter syntax (e.g., protocol types, operators, values) to improve readability and help users quickly identify syntax errors.  
4. Filter Templates: Provide a library of customizable filter templates for common use cases, such as troubleshooting specific network issues or analyzing common protocols.  
5. Graphical Filter Builder: Develop a drag-and-drop interface for building filters, allowing users to select protocols, fields, and operators from a graphical menu.  
6. Smart Error Handling: Implement intelligent error messages that not only highlight syntax errors but also suggest corrections and provide explanations.  
7. Filter Sharing and Collaboration: Create a platform for sharing custom filters within the Wireshark community, allowing users to rate and comment on the effectiveness of shared filters.  
8. Historical Filter Analysis: Offer a feature that analyzes the user's filter history to suggest optimizations or identify frequently used filters that could be automated.  
9. Integrated Protocol Documentation: Embed protocol documentation directly within the filter interface, allowing users to hover over elements for detailed explanations and examples.  
10. Contextual Help: Provide context-sensitive help and tips that appear as users build filters, offering guidance based on the current focus of the filter construction.  
11. Voice Command Filtering: Introduce voice recognition capabilities to allow users to construct or modify filters using voice commands.  
12. Regular Expression Support: Enhance filters with full support for regular expressions, enabling more complex and powerful search capabilities.  
13. Filter by Example: Allow users to select specific packets and automatically generate a filter that matches similar packets, facilitating easier setup for complex filters.  
14. Machine Learning Optimizations: Use machine learning to suggest filter optimizations based on the analysis of large datasets and user filtering habits.  
15. Customizable Interface: Enable users to customize the layout and functionality of the filter interface, including the ability to create custom keyboard shortcuts for frequent actions.  
16. Protocol-Specific Filtering Wizards: Offer guided wizards for creating filters for specific protocols, simplifying the process of setting up complex filters.  
17. Multi-Condition Builder: Introduce a more intuitive interface for creating filters with multiple conditions, including logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) in a visual format.  
18. Real-Time Filter Preview: Implement a feature that previews the effect of a filter on the dataset in real-time, before applying it to the entire capture.  
19. Filter Import/Export: Provide functionality to easily import and export filters in a standardized format, facilitating sharing and collaboration beyond the Wireshark platform.  
20. Interactive Tutorial Mode: Create an interactive tutorial for the filter feature, guiding new users through the process of constructing various types of filters.  
21. Advanced Analytics Integration: Integrate advanced analytics features, such as statistical analysis and pattern detection, directly into the filter construction process.  
22. Personalized Filter Recommendations: Develop an AI-driven recommendation system that suggests filters based on the user's specific interests and the characteristics of the captured data.  
23. Cross-Session Filter Management: Enable users to save, manage, and apply filters across different Wireshark sessions, including synchronization across devices.  
24. Filter Debugging Tool: Introduce a debugging tool specifically for filters, allowing users to step through each part of the filter logic to identify and resolve issues.  
25. Augmented Reality (AR) Filter Construction: Explore the use of AR for filter construction, allowing users to visualize and manipulate packet flows and filter criteria in a three-dimensional space.
